title: Κηπωρὸς καὶ κύων
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 155. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A gardener's dog fell into a well.
sentences.n: Chambry spells the word κηπωρός here with an ω, where the fable just before has κηπουρός; the two spellings stand for the same trade, and the page is followed as it stands. φρέαρ is a dug well, distinct from a spring.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ κηπωρὸς βουλόμενος αὐτὸν ἐκεῖθεν ἀνενεγκεῖν, κατῆλθε καὶ αὐτὸς εἰς τὸ φρέαρ.
sentences.tr: Ho de kēpōros boulomenos auton ekeithen anenenkein, katēlthe kai autos eis to phrear.
sentences.l: And the gardener, wishing to bring him up out of there, went down himself as well into the well.
sentences.n: ἀνενεγκεῖν is the aorist infinitive of ἀναφέρω, "carry up"; its stem looks nothing like the present. καὶ αὐτός is "he too, for his part".

sentences.t: Οἰηθεὶς δ’ ὁ κύων ὡς κατωτέρω μᾶλλον αὐτὸν παραγέγονε καταδῦσαι, τὸν κηπωρὸν στραφεὶς ἔδακεν.
sentences.tr: Oiētheis d’ ho kyōn hōs katōterō mallon auton paragegone katadysai, ton kēpōron strapheis edaken.
sentences.l: But the dog, having supposed that he had come to sink him yet further down, turning, bit the gardener.
sentences.i: But the dog took it that the man had come to push him under deeper still, and so turned and bit him.
sentences.n: οἰηθείς is the aorist passive in form of the deponent οἴομαι, "having supposed"; στραφείς is the aorist passive of στρέφω used intransitively, "having turned round". ὡς introduces what he supposed, with the perfect παραγέγονε left in the indicative. μᾶλλον reinforces the comparative κατωτέρω: further down still. καταδῦσαι is transitive here: to sink someone, not to sink oneself.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ μετ’ ὀδύνης ἐπανιών· « Δίκαια, φησί, πέπονθα· τί δήποτε γὰρ τὸν αὐτόχειρα σῶσαι ἐσπούδασα ; »
sentences.tr: Ho de met’ odynēs epaniōn· « Dikaia, phēsi, pepontha· ti dēpote gar ton autocheira sōsai espoudasa ; »
sentences.l: And he, coming back up in pain: « Justly, says he, have I suffered; for why on earth was I eager to save one who was his own destroyer? »
sentences.i: And as he climbed back up in pain: « I have suffered no more than I deserved, says he; for whatever possessed me to rescue a creature who had brought it on himself? »
sentences.n: The participle ἐπανιών is left standing without a finite verb of its own; the φησί set inside the speech carries the sentence, which is the ordinary Greek way of marking a quotation. δίκαια is a neuter plural accusative, the internal object of πέπονθα — "I have suffered just things" — which English turns into the adverb "justly". αὐτόχειρ is literally "with one's own hand", used of a man who does a deed himself, most often a killing, and so of one who is his own destroyer: the dog's fall was his own doing. The word could as well be aimed at the bite just given, and the Greek leaves the choice open. Chambry sets a space before the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος πρὸς ἀδίκους καὶ ἀχαρίστους.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos pros adikous kai acharistous.
sentences.l: The fable is directed at unjust and thankless men.
sentences.n: The closing formula has no verb at all: πρός with the accusative simply names the people the fable is aimed at.
